client: I've been really struggling since my dad passed away two months ago. Every time there's a family gathering, it just hits me all over again — like I walk in and expect to see him there, and then I remember he's not, and it's like losing him all over again. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help, honestly, because nothing's going to bring him back.
therapist: What you're carrying sounds deeply painful — that moment of walking in and expecting to see him, only to be met with his absence again, is such a heartbreaking kind of grief to live through. You're right that nothing will bring him back, and I want you to know I'm not here to pretend otherwise or offer easy fixes. I'm curious though — when you say you're not sure talking will help, what would "help" even look like for you right now, if you could imagine it?

client: Honestly, I don't even know what help would look like. I think part of me just wants to stop dreading those family gatherings, or at least not feel like I'm blindsided every single time by this wave of grief. But even saying that out loud feels kind of pointless, because I don't see how talking about it changes what happens when I walk through that door.
therapist: It makes a lot of sense that you'd want some relief from that wave catching you off guard each time — that's not a small thing to wish for, and it's actually a really meaningful starting point. You're right that talking won't change what's behind that door, but sometimes it can gently shift what's happening *inside* you as you walk through it — the thoughts and expectations your mind is holding in that moment. I'm wondering, when you're approaching one of those gatherings, what does your mind tend to tell you in the moments before you arrive?

client: Before I even get there, my mind kind of goes quiet in this weird way, like I'm bracing for impact. I think somewhere in the back of my head I'm still half-expecting to see him sitting in his usual chair, even though I know logically that's not going to happen. And then there's this guilt that creeps in too, like maybe if I just prepared myself better or thought about it differently, it wouldn't hit me so hard — like I'm failing at grieving somehow.
therapist: That image of your mind going quiet and bracing for impact is so vivid, and it tells me how much weight you're carrying into those moments even before anything has happened. I want to gently push back on something though — the idea that you're "failing at grieving" is a really common thought, but grief doesn't actually come with a rulebook, and the fact that part of you still expects to see him in his chair isn't a failure, it's a testament to how real and present he was in your life. What do you think he would say if he heard you blaming yourself for not grieving "well enough"?

client: He would probably tell me to stop being so hard on myself — that was kind of his thing, actually, always telling me I expected too much from myself. But hearing that framing right now almost makes it worse in a way, because it reminds me of exactly the kind of thing he would say, and he's not here to say it anymore. I don't know, maybe that's useful somehow, but right now it just feels like another reminder of what I've lost.
therapist: That's such a tender and bittersweet thing to notice — that even the comfort his words might offer carries its own ache right now, because it leads you straight back to missing him. I don't want to rush past that, because what you just described actually feels really important: his voice is still *with* you in some way, even if that's painful to sit with right now. I'm wondering, over time, do you think that same voice — the one that tells you to stop being so hard on yourself — could ever feel more like a connection to him rather than just a reminder of his absence?

client: Maybe, but that feels really far away right now, like something I can't even picture yet. I want to believe that his voice in my head could feel like a comfort someday instead of just a wound, but I honestly don't know how you get from here to there. It feels a little like you're asking me to imagine the end of a tunnel when I'm still standing in the dark.
therapist: That image of standing in the dark in the tunnel is so honest, and I don't want to pull you toward a light you can't see yet — that's not where you are right now, and that's okay. What you're describing — just being in the dark, not knowing how to get through — is actually exactly where grief often lives in these early months, and there's no shortcut through it. I'm curious, is there anything, even something small, that has felt even slightly easier to carry in the two months since you lost him — any moment, however brief, where the weight lifted even a little?

client: There was one evening a few weeks ago where my brother and I ended up just sitting around talking about my dad — like telling old stories, some of them funny ones — and for a little while it felt okay, almost good even. But then afterward I felt guilty about it, like I had somehow betrayed my grief by laughing, or like enjoying a memory meant I was forgetting how much I miss him. So even that moment that felt lighter came with its own kind of weight attached to it.
therapist: That evening with your brother sounds genuinely precious — laughter and love and grief all tangled up together, which is actually such a human way to honor someone. The guilt that followed makes a lot of sense, but I want to offer a gentle reframe: what if enjoying that memory isn't a betrayal of your grief, but actually one of the truest expressions of how much he mattered to you — that his stories are still alive enough to make you laugh? I'm wondering, do you think your dad would have wanted you to feel guilty for that moment, or something else?

client: No, he definitely wouldn't have wanted me to feel guilty — he would have loved knowing that my brother and I were sitting around laughing about him, that's exactly the kind of thing he lived for. But knowing that in my head and actually feeling it in my gut are two completely different things, and I think that's where I keep getting stuck. The reframe makes sense logically, but I don't know how to make my feelings catch up to what I know is true.
therapist: You've just named something really central to how our minds work — that gap between what we *know* and what we *feel* is one of the most frustrating parts of being human, and it's not a flaw in you, it's just how emotions operate, they tend to change through experience and repetition rather than logic alone. What's actually hopeful here is that you already *have* an experience — that evening with your brother — where your feelings and your love for him briefly aligned in a way that felt okay, even good. I'm wondering if it might be worth thinking about how you could create more small moments like that one, not to force the feelings to catch up, but to gently give them more chances to?

client: I like the idea in theory, but I'm also a little scared of it — like what if I try to recreate that kind of moment with my brother and it just doesn't land the same way, and then I feel worse instead of better. That evening happened kind of naturally, we weren't trying to do anything, we just fell into it, and I worry that if I make it intentional it'll feel forced or hollow. I don't want to turn something that felt real into some kind of therapy exercise.
therapist: That fear makes complete sense, and I want to be clear — I'm not suggesting you manufacture something or follow a script, because you're right that the realness of that evening is exactly what made it meaningful. It's less about recreating it and more about simply being open to it happening again, maybe just by spending unhurried time with your brother without any agenda, and trusting that your shared love for your dad might find its own way into the conversation. I'm curious, is there anything that feels like a natural, low-pressure reason you and your brother might just *be* together sometime soon — not to do grief, just to be family?

client: Actually, we've been talking about going through some of my dad's old stuff together — there are boxes in my mom's garage that nobody's dealt with yet. That feels like a natural reason to be together, but honestly it also terrifies me because I don't know what we'll find in those boxes or how it'll feel. I guess it could go either way — it could be one of those moments where something real happens, or it could just be really, really hard.
therapist: It sounds like you're holding both the fear and the possibility of that moment at the same time, which actually takes a quiet kind of courage — and the fact that you can see it could go either way tells me you're approaching it with real honesty rather than dread alone. Going through those boxes with your brother might be hard, and it might also be exactly the kind of unscripted, real moment where your dad shows up again in the best way — through an old photo, a handwritten note, something that makes you both laugh or cry or both. What do you think would help you feel even a little more ready to say yes to that, when the time comes?

client: I think what would help is knowing that my brother and I don't have to finish everything in one go, that we can stop if it gets to be too much and that's okay. I guess I have this fear that once we start we'll feel obligated to push through even if it becomes overwhelming, and that pressure makes it feel harder to begin at all. Maybe if I talked to him beforehand and we agreed it was okay to take breaks or even just walk away for the day, that might make it feel less like something I have to survive and more like something we're doing together at our own pace.
therapist: You've just figured something really important out on your own — that what makes this feel survivable isn't pushing through, but having permission to be human about it, to go at your own pace with someone you trust beside you. That conversation with your brother beforehand isn't just practical, it's actually a way of honoring your dad together before you even open a single box. I'm wondering, does it feel like something you could reach out to your brother about soon — not to set a date necessarily, but just to have that conversation and see how it feels?
